short: The share of your available capacity that was actually booked and used.
seoTitle: Utilisation Rate — Formula and Worked Example
metaDescription: Utilisation rate measures booked hours against available capacity, the core number for any business that sells time. Formula, example and how to read it.
definition: Utilisation rate is the proportion of a business's available capacity that was actually used, expressed as a percentage — booked and delivered hours divided by the hours that were there to sell.

formula.expression: Utilisation rate = (booked hours ÷ available capacity hours) × 100
formula.note: Available capacity is service positions multiplied by open hours multiplied by days in the period. Count delivered hours, not booked-and-missed ones, if you want the number to reflect earnings.

bodyHtml:
What it tells a business that sells time

A salon chair, a consulting room, a treatment table, a billable hour and a workshop bay are all the same thing economically: capacity that expires. Unlike stock, an unsold hour cannot be sold tomorrow. Utilisation rate is the one number that puts a figure on how much of it expired unsold.

Working it out

Take the period, count the capacity, divide the delivered durations into it. Two chairs open nine hours a day for six days is 108 chair-hours in a week; 69 hours of delivered appointments against that is a utilisation rate of 64%, leaving 39 hours of rent and wages that earned nothing.

Reading it properly

The headline percentage matters less than its shape. Empty capacity is rarely spread evenly — it clusters in particular slots, particular days, particular staff. A business at 64% overall might be at 95% on Saturday and 30% on Tuesday morning, and those two numbers call for completely different responses: pricing or staffing on one, promotion on the other. Very high utilisation is not automatically good either, since a business running at 95% has no room to absorb a rush and nothing left to sell.

faq.question: What is a good utilisation rate?
faq.answer: It depends on the cost of standing still. Rather than chase a benchmark, multiply your empty hours by what a delivered hour contributes after variable cost, and compare that against the rent and wages those hours carried. That gives you a figure to act on instead of a percentage to feel bad about.

faq.question: Should no-shows count as utilised capacity?
faq.answer: Not if you want the number to track earnings. A booked slot that nobody turned up for cost you exactly as much as an empty one, so count delivered hours in the numerator and track no-shows separately — the two problems have different fixes.
